passage: The kitchen was full of aunties, and the pressure cooker kept hissing. Gurleen Bua shouted over the noise, "Ujjwal, get the steel plates from the top shelf, wipe them, and take twelve to the terrace. Then tell Dadaji food is in ten minutes." Ujjwal, nine, nodded, lips moving: "Plates, wipe, twelve, terrace, Dadaji." He wiped the plates, counted twelve and carried them upstairs. On the stairs, a cousin asked him to play cricket. "After," he said, still muttering. He set the plates down, then found Dadaji on his chair. "Ten minutes, Dadaji." Then he ran off to play.

qa.q: How many plates did Gurleen Bua ask Ujjwal to take?
qa.a: She asked him to take twelve plates.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal keep muttering the steps?
qa.a: He wanted to hold all the instructions in mind in the noisy kitchen and was worried about forgetting one halfway.

qa.q: What could Gurleen Bua do to make multi-step jobs easier in a noisy place?
qa.a: Say the steps slowly, or ask Ujjwal to repeat them back once before he starts.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Ujjwal says "After"?
qa.a: He may be a little disappointed, but he gets to play once Ujjwal finishes his tasks.

grounding: It shows a nine-year-old holding a four-step instruction in memory through noise and a distraction.

passage: In Class 4 of a Chennai school, Vandana Ma'am gave instructions for the leaf project: "Collect five different leaves, press them in a notebook for two days, paste them on chart paper, and write each tree's name underneath." Kamal, ten, used to forget half of what she said. This time he wrote four words on his palm in pen: collect, press, paste, name. At home he copied them onto paper and ticked them off one by one. On Monday his chart had all five leaves and their names, though the neem label was spelt wrong. He grinned when Ma'am held it up.

qa.q: Which four words did Kamal write on his palm?
qa.a: Collect, press, paste and name.

qa.q: Why might Kamal have written the words on his palm this time?
qa.a: He was worried about forgetting long instructions again and wanted to make sure he didn't miss a step.

qa.q: How could Vandana Ma'am help the whole class with long tasks?
qa.a: She could write the steps on the board or on a slip, so children like Kamal can check them.

qa.q: How might Kamal's parents notice a change at home?
qa.a: They would see him working through the project step by step on his own instead of asking what to do next.

grounding: It shows a child using a memory aid to follow a multi-step school instruction he used to forget.

passage:
"Mehak, can you make lemonade while I rest?" asked Rajni Nani.
"Yes! Tell me."
"Squeeze two lemons into the jug. Add four spoons of sugar. Fill water to the blue line. Stir till the sugar hides. Then a pinch of salt."
Mehak counted on her fingers. "Lemons, sugar, water, stir, salt."
Ten minutes later: "Nani, taste!"
Rajni sipped. "Sweet and sour. Did you add salt?"
Mehak's eyes widened. "Oh! I stopped at stir." She added a pinch. "Now five out of five."
"Last month you forgot three steps," Nani said, smiling.
"This month only one!"

qa.q: How many spoons of sugar did Nani say to add?
qa.a: Four spoons of sugar.

qa.q: What does Mehak counting on her fingers suggest she was worried about?
qa.a: She seemed worried about forgetting a step, so she counted them on her fingers and said them back as five short words.

qa.q: What could Mehak try next time to avoid missing the last step?
qa.a: Fold one finger down after each step as she does it, so she can see which step is left.

qa.q: What would change if Nani gave the instructions one step at a time?
qa.a: Mehak would forget less, but she would get less practice holding a whole list in her head. 😊

grounding: It shows a child holding a five-step recipe in working memory and improving from month to month.

passage: When I was eight, Kashish Akka would tell me, 'Bring the bucket, fill it halfway, add the soap, then bring the mug.' I'd come back with just the bucket. She'd sigh. This year, in science, Ma'am gave us five steps to grow a bean. I whispered them to myself and counted on my fingers: soak, wrap, wet, dark, check. I didn't miss one, even when my partner kept chatting about cricket. My bean sprouted first, and I felt ten feet tall.

qa.q: How many steps did the teacher give for growing a bean?
qa.a: She gave five steps.

qa.q: Why did the narrator whisper the steps and count on their fingers?
qa.a: They were anxious not to forget a step as they used to, so they held all five in mind by whispering and counting.

qa.q: What memory trick could the narrator teach a younger child?
qa.a: They could teach saying the steps quietly and counting them on fingers, since that helped them follow multi-step instructions.

qa.q: How might Kashish Akka see the narrator's change?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased and relieved that her younger sibling can now follow longer instructions.

grounding: Illustrates a child developing working memory to follow multi-step instructions over time.

passage:
Classroom note by Nirmala Ma'am, Class 3
In June, Urmila could only follow one step at a time and often drifted off during group work. Today I gave three steps: take out your ruler, draw a square, colour one half. She did all three while I watched, then checked her work against the board without being reminded. She stayed on her task for the full twenty minutes. When I said well done, she looked shyly pleased. 😊

qa.q: How many steps did Nirmala Ma'am give today?
qa.a: She gave three steps.

qa.q: What does Urmila looking shyly pleased suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud of her progress but a little embarrassed by the praise.

qa.q: How could Nirmala Ma'am keep building Urmila's attention?
qa.a: She could slowly add a fourth step and keep praising her effort, not just the result.

qa.q: How might Urmila's group-work partners notice the change?
qa.a: They may find her more helpful and focused, and enjoy working with her more.

grounding: Shows a child's growing attention span and ability to follow multi-step instructions, noted by a teacher.

passage:
Uma's diary, Thursday
Science was fun! Sachin Sir gave us four steps all at once: put the seed on the cotton, pour two spoons of water, cover with the plate, and write your name on the label. Last month I'd only remember the first step. This time I counted the steps on my fingers while he talked. I did them in order, and my seed was the first one ready. Sir said, "Well listened, Uma." I felt tall.

qa.q: How many spoons of water did they pour?
qa.a: Two spoons of water.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Sir said "Well listened, Uma"?
qa.a: Uma felt proud and tall, happy that the finger trick had worked.

qa.q: What could Uma try when instructions get even longer?
qa.a: Keep using the finger-counting trick, or repeat the steps quietly to herself.

qa.q: How might Sachin Sir see Uma's progress since last month?
qa.a: He'd likely be pleased she can now remember and follow all four steps in order.

grounding: Shows a child's growing attention and memory as she follows four-step instructions using a finger-counting trick.

passage: Before he left for the weekly market in their town, Kunal's mother Uma gave him three jobs. "Buy two coconuts, give this letter to the tailor, and collect Nani's glasses from the optician." Kunal, nine, used to forget the middle one. This time he said it back to her in order, then repeated it under his breath as he walked. At the tailor's he nearly forgot the letter, then patted his pocket and remembered. He came home with everything.

qa.q: How many coconuts did Kunal need to buy?
qa.a: Two coconuts.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he patted his pocket at the tailor's?
qa.a: He had a moment of worry that he'd forgotten, then relief when he remembered.

qa.q: What small step helped Kunal remember all three jobs?
qa.a: Saying them back in order and repeating them as he walked.

qa.q: How might Uma feel when Kunal comes home with everything?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that he managed all three jobs on his own.

grounding: Shows a child holding three errands in memory and carrying them out in order.

passage: In Mei's kitchen in Sydney, her grandmother read the dumpling recipe out loud once, then went to answer the phone. "Flour, water, knead for five minutes, rest, then roll," she called. Dalia, ten, and Mei looked at each other. "What was after knead?" Mei asked. "Rest," said Dalia, counting on her fingers. "Then roll." They did it step by step, and when her grandmother came back, the dough was resting under a cloth.

qa.q: How long did they knead the dough?
qa.a: For five minutes.

qa.q: What might Mei have felt when she asked "What was after knead?"
qa.a: She seemed unsure and a little anxious about forgetting a step.

qa.q: How could the girls make it easier next time?
qa.a: Write the steps down or repeat them aloud together before starting.

qa.q: How might Mei's grandmother feel when she sees the dough resting?
qa.a: Pleased and impressed that they followed the steps on their own.

grounding: Shows children holding a multi-step recipe in memory and following it in order.

passage: The school lab in Hubballi smelled of vinegar. Kunal Sir said: "Listen carefully. Put two spoons of soda in the cup. Add a little vinegar. Watch the bubbles. Then write what you saw." He said it only once. Kishore, ten, whispered the steps under his breath, "soda, vinegar, watch, write," tapping one finger for each. Last term he always forgot the last step. Today he did all four in order and wrote "fizz, then foam, then quiet." He looked up at Kunal Sir, smiling.

qa.q: How many spoons of soda were they told to put in the cup?
qa.a: Two spoons.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he looked up at Kunal Sir?
qa.a: He felt proud and satisfied at completing all four steps correctly.

qa.q: What strategy helped Kishore remember the steps?
qa.a: He whispered the steps to himself and tapped a finger for each one.

qa.q: How might Kunal Sir see Kishore's improvement since last term?
qa.a: He would likely be pleased to see Kishore remember all the steps without reminders.

grounding: A ten-year-old uses a whispered, finger-tap method to hold four lab steps in mind.

passage: I'm Leela. On Saturday I watched my brother Akash, eleven, make lemon rice for the first time. Amma read the steps once from the old notebook: rinse the rice, heat the oil, add mustard seeds, then the curry leaves, then the lemon at the very end. Last year he'd forget halfway and ask again. This time he said them back to Amma first, then went step by step without looking at the notebook. Only once did he pause, spoon in the air, eyes closed, before reaching for the curry leaves. I don't know what he was thinking, but it tasted right.

qa.q: What was added at the very end?
qa.a: The lemon.

qa.q: What does Akash pausing with eyes closed suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was concentrating hard, perhaps a little unsure, trying to remember the next step.

qa.q: What helped Akash follow the recipe this time?
qa.a: He said the steps back to Amma first, which helped him hold them in mind.

qa.q: How does Leela see her brother's cooking compared with last year?
qa.a: Leela notices he no longer forgets halfway and can do it without asking again.

grounding: A sister watches her brother follow a multi-step recipe from memory.

passage:
Week 1: At football practice, Coach Rekha said, "Dribble to the cone, pass to Kamal, run to the flag, then back." Kamal, nine, got to the cone and stopped, scratching his head. "What next?"
Week 3: Rekha gave the steps again. Kamal said them back, "cone, pass, flag, back," and did three of the four before looking around.
Week 6: Rekha smiled and said she was adding a fifth step: a shot at goal. Kamal listened, nodded, and did all five without stopping, then jogged back, beaming. "I didn't forget anything!"

qa.q: How many steps did Kamal do in Week 6?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when he said, "I didn't forget anything!"?
qa.a: He felt proud and delighted with himself.

qa.q: What helped Kamal get better at following the drill?
qa.a: Saying the steps back to himself and practising the same drill over weeks.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel about Kamal's progress by Week 6?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged to see him manage longer instructions.

grounding: Over six weeks, a nine-year-old gets better at following a multi-step football drill.

passage:
Sachin, come sit. You say you forget what your teacher tells you after the second step? Let your Alka Bua tell you about the halwa.

When I was ten, my mother was ill in bed one Diwali and said, "Alka, make the halwa. First roast the sooji in ghee, then add sugar, then water, then stir till thick, then cardamom." Five steps. I forgot the third before she'd finished.

So I went back and said, "Tell me again, slowly." This time I held up one finger for each step and repeated them out loud. Sooji, ghee. Sugar. Water. Stir. Cardamom.

In the kitchen I said each one before I did it. It came out lumpy but edible, and she laughed and ate two bowls.

So, Sachin, use your fingers. Say it as you go.

qa.q: How many steps did the halwa have?
qa.a: Five steps.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel when she forgot the third step?
qa.a: Young Alka probably felt worried and flustered, afraid of spoiling the halwa while her mother was ill.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Alka's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Asking her mother to repeat slowly and holding up one finger per step helped her remember the steps in order.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother have felt eating the halwa?
qa.a: Her mother was likely touched and proud, laughing and eating two bowls.

grounding: An aunt tells how, at ten, she learned to follow multi-step instructions by repeating them and counting steps on her fingers.

passage:
During the monsoon, the power went off in the house near Guwahati, and the rain was pouring. Bhupen called to Ramesh, ten, from the kitchen.

"Ramesh, get the torch from the top drawer, then the candles from the shelf, then the matchbox from the kitchen, and bring them to the living room."

Ramesh repeated it under his breath. "Torch, drawer. Candles, shelf. Matches, kitchen. Living room."

He found the torch first and used it to light his way. Then the candles. Then the matchbox. He brought them all to the living room.

Bhupen smiled. "All four steps in the dark. Well done."

qa.q: Where were the candles?
qa.a: The candles were on the shelf.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel finding everything in the dark?
qa.a: Ramesh was probably a bit nervous in the dark, but focused and proud when he got it right.

qa.q: What helped Ramesh remember all the steps?
qa.a: He repeated the steps under his breath and used the torch to help with the next ones.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel when Ramesh brought everything?
qa.a: Bhupen was likely pleased and proud of him.

grounding: During a monsoon power cut, a child follows a four-step instruction in the dark by repeating it to himself.

passage:
The last science lab before the Christmas holidays at the school in Pune was noisy. Samir Sir gave instructions quickly.

"Fill the cup halfway with water. Add two spoons of salt. Stir. Drop in the egg. Watch what happens. Write it down."

Vaibhav, nine, counted on his fingers as Samir Sir spoke. Six steps. He whispered them again to his partner.

They followed each step. The egg floated.

"It floats!" Vaibhav shouted. He wrote it down, the last step.

Samir Sir looked over. "You didn't miss a single step."

qa.q: What happened to the egg?
qa.a: The egg floated.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when the egg floated?
qa.a: Vaibhav was excited and thrilled, shouting that it floats.

qa.q: What helped Vaibhav remember the six steps?
qa.a: He counted them on his fingers and whispered them to his partner.

qa.q: How might Samir Sir feel seeing Vaibhav's work?
qa.a: Samir Sir was likely impressed and pleased that no step was missed.

grounding: In a noisy science lab, a child follows a six-step instruction by counting and repeating the steps.

passage:
"Okay, Rafiq, listen to all four steps before you touch anything," said Manoj, spreading kite paper on the terrace two days before Uttarayan.
"First, fold the paper corner to corner. Second, glue the long stick down the fold. Third, bend the thin stick across and tie it. Fourth, trim the extra paper."
"Got it."
"Say them back."
"Fold, glue the long stick, bend and tie the thin one... and cut the extra."
"Good. Last year you forgot after step one."
Rafiq worked slowly, whispering, "Third... tie it." His kite came out a little crooked, but it held.
"Will it fly?"
"Tomorrow we test it," said Manoj.

qa.q: How many steps did Manoj explain?
qa.a: Manoj explained four steps.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq whisper "Third... tie it" while working?
qa.a: He was concentrating hard to keep the steps in mind, determined not to lose track this year.

qa.q: What part of Manoj's teaching helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Rafiq to say the steps back helped him hold all four in memory before starting.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel seeing Rafiq finish the kite?
qa.a: Manoj would likely feel pleased and proud, remembering that Rafiq forgot after step one only last year.

grounding: Illustrates a child's growing working memory as he holds and follows a four-step kite-making instruction.
